docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This block diagram illustrates the individual subsystem for the user buttons and temperature readings for the Radiolink. This includes how major components of the subsystem are connected, how the power is distributed, and how signals travel between the subsystem and the rest of the team’s device. The subsystem is powered from a shared 5V voltage located on Sultan's board, providing power to the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, the MCP9700A temperature sensor, the MCP6004 operational amplifier, and the buttons. The MCP9700A temperature sensor produces an analog voltage signal that passes through the MCP6004, configured as a non-inverting amplifier, to amplify the signal sent to the PIC’s RA0/ADC input for measurement. The non-inverting configuration increases the sensor's output voltage while maintaining its polarity, improving the signal's usable range for ADC measurements. All the user inputs are provided through six buttons connected to digital input pins on the microcontroller. Communication with the rest of the team occurs through Connector 2, which provides RX, TX, 5 V, and GND, allowing both power distribution and bidirectional UART communication between subsystems.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Temperature Sensor

  1. Microchip Technologies MCP9700A-E/TO

    • $0.61/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Cost effective Requires ADC conversion Easy through-hole soldering Analog signal susceptible to noise Direct PIC ADC connection

  2. Texas Instruments TMP36GT9Z

    • $1.85/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Wide temperature range Higher cost Simple analog interface Lower specified accuracy at 25°C Compatible with 5V supply

  3. Texas Instruments TMP235A2DBZR

    !

    • $0.56/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Cost effective Difficult for surface-mount soldering Small PCB footprint Different voltage-to-temperature conversion Good specified accuracy (±1.2°C (±2°C))

Choice: Option 1: MCP9700A-E/TO

Rationale: The MCP9700A is not only cost effective, but provides simple and direct integration for the Curiosity Nano that will be used for this part of the product. Although its readings aren't as accurate at the TMP235A2DBZR, readings are still within a ±2°C range, and will have a more reliable method of installation.

Operational Amplifier

  1. Microchip Technologies MCP6004-I/SL

    • $0.53/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Low power consumption supports an efficient subsystem Lower slew rate than the alternatives. SOIC-14 package is manageable for PCB assembly Four amplifiers may be unnecessary if only one temperature signal needs conditioning. Operates directly from the subsystem's 5 V supply

  2. Texas Instruments TLV9004IDR

    ![Op-Amp](

    • $0.91/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Lower typical supply current than MCP6004 Four channels may be unnecessary for the current circuit. Includes EMI/RFI filtering features Maximum supply voltage is limited to 5.5 V. Lower maximum input offset voltage improves potential measurement accuracy

  3. Texas Instruments TLV9054IDR

    • $1.14/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons 5 MHz bandwidth provides room for future applications Higher power consumption than very low-power alternatives Low input offset voltage supports accurate sensing Higher bandwidth is unnecessary for slow temperature measurements Available in SOIC-14 for PCB integration

Choice: Option 1: MCP6004-I/SL

Rationale: The MCP6004 was selected as the best operational amplifier for the subsystem for its effective balance between low power consumption, cost-effectiveness, and compatibility with the subsystem's design. Its operating voltage range of 1.8–6 V allows it to function reliably with the team's regulated 5 V power supply. Additionally, its rail-to-rail input and output capabilities make it suitable for amplifying the MCP9700A temperature sensor's analog voltage through a non-inverting amplifier configuration before sending the signal to the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano's ADC. In comparison, the TLV9054IDR and TLV9004IDR lack the advantages that the MCP6004 holds.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is designed to support an individual subsystem that reads surrounding temperature, and communicates with other team members' boards. This system uses an MCP9700-E/TO to measure the temperature, while an MCP6004 operational amplifier conditions & amplifies the analog signal before the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller processes it. Additionally, this subsystem includes 4 directional buttons (FWD, BACK, LEFT, RIGHT), and 2 action buttons (ENTER, BACK), for user input, while a test button and LED may be used for debugging and verification. Power is supplied through a regulated 5V system, as capacitors are used to stabilize power and for signal filtering. UART communication is also used through RA3 and RA4 to transmit and receive information between the other subsystems of the project.

Figure 1: Subsystem schematic for function buttons and temperature sensor.
